what: Where each frame's time goes inside the immersive session on a Meta Quest 3S, Quest Browser, both hands tracked, on the live site. Read by a three-second probe attached over the Chrome DevTools Protocol (tmp/q-prof.js, tmp/q-sys.js, tmp/q-input.js in the working tree): it times the session's frame callback, each render pass and each system's update, then removes itself. The budget at the headset's 90 Hz is 11.1 ms a frame.

found: The hand rays walked 2,553 scene nodes a frame for each hand: 70 interactable roots, 60 of them pieces off the set, every piece twice because the slate that holds them is interactable too, and all five poses of each actor.
Three actors were 69 of the 163 draw calls, the slate's striped edge 24, the camera 16.
The monitor's lens view was redrawn on every frame while anything moved, on top of the shadow pass.
With both hands out of view the same set ran at 90.

after.note: Six three-second readings 20 s apart in a session of two and a half minutes. The same six pieces as before; from the second reading on the truck had been stretched to 191% by hand, and in the last two a second camera was on the set.
found: Better, not 90: 73 to 82 frames a second with both hands tracked against 66 to 68, and 7.8 to 9.2 ms of JavaScript a frame against 12.8.
The input pass (hand rays and fingertip pointers) still cost 2.2 to 3.3 ms a frame in five of the six readings with hands tracked, and a quarter of a millisecond with the hands out of view.

Timed afterwards in the emulator, half of that pass is the panel: some 280 small meshes that each hand's ray and each fingertip try on every frame. The next build closes the panel to the pointers unless a hand points at it or reaches for it (3.3 ms to 1.7 ms a frame in the emulator). That is not yet measured on the headset.
